title: They differ
hook: rebirth, resurrection, return, nothing, mystery: kept apart, each in its home
carry: each stays in its own home

segments.voice: Yesterday, the other end of life: welcoming birth. Your line was welcome. Did someone new get a welcome from you? Today, back to the end, and to the answers, one at a time. Day eight hundred seventeen.

Five doors in one hallway, each with a different name on it. Behind one, a life comes back in a new body. Behind another, the dead are raised. Behind the third, the spirit goes back to where it came from. The fourth opens onto nothing at all. The fifth won't open, and the people who built it say that is the honest answer. For weeks now this block has walked past each door, one at a time. Today we stand in the hallway, look at all five, and don't knock down a single wall between them.
screen: `FIVE DOORS, ONE HALLWAY.` → `NO WALLS KNOCKED DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, rebirth. Buddhists teach rebirth shaped by karma, without a fixed soul passing from life to life. The Bhagavad Gita gives a Hindu picture: as a person casts off worn clothes and puts on new ones, the self casts off worn bodies. Two homes, two vocabularies, and they don't say the same thing. Second, resurrection. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Martha, "I am the resurrection, and the life." Christians hope for the raising of the dead. The Qur'an says every soul shall taste death, and speaks of a Day of Resurrection when each soul is paid what it earned. Third, return. Ecclesiastes says, "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." At Sikh funerals the bedtime prayer, Kirtan Sohila, is sung, and death is spoken of as going home. Fourth, nothing, or mystery. Lucretius taught that the ages after death will trouble us no more than the ages before birth. Socrates kept two options open: dreamless sleep, or a journey. Confucius, asked about death, turned the question back to life. So the block lands here: they differ. Set a Buddhist teacher's answer beside a Christian priest's, and this path doesn't read them as two versions of one answer. Each answer lives inside a whole way of life, with its own texts, rites and hopes. Pulled out and blended, each one loses what makes it make sense. So each stays in its own home, and anyone can visit.
screen: `FIRST, REBIRTH.` · `SECOND, RESURRECTION.` · `THIRD, RETURN.` · `FOURTH, NOTHING, OR MYSTERY.` · then, large: `THEY DIFFER.`

segments.voice: Take a pen, or open a note. On the first day of this block, the invitation was to write what you think now. Today, write again, a few lines only: what do you think happens at death, or what do you honestly not know? Use your own words, not a borrowed sentence, unless that sentence really is yours. If you kept what you wrote on that first day, you can set the two side by side later, without grading either one. When the lines are done, put the pen down and sit quietly with them. The bell holds the time.
They differ. Rebirth, resurrection, return, nothing, mystery: real answers from real traditions, each kept in its own home, never blended into one. Today's word.
Your line: each stays in its own home. Today, if death comes up in conversation, ask someone what their tradition says, and listen without fitting it into yours. Day eight hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Traditions teach different things about death: Buddhists and Hindus speak of rebirth in their own distinct ways, Christians and Muslims of resurrection and judgment, Sikhs of going home, and some philosophers of nothing at all. Interfaith settings often let each speak for itself.

notes: Each tradition's answer is summarized in one or two sentences; Keepers of each path should confirm their summary is fair and not flattened (especially Buddhist rebirth without a fixed soul, and the Hindu picture from Gita 2.22).
Qur'an 3:185 paraphrased (every soul shall taste death; paid in full on the Day of Resurrection); confirm.
Jewish teaching on the afterlife (resurrection of the dead in Jewish liturgy, olam ha-ba) is not named among the five; consider whether a Judaism Keeper wants it named under resurrection.
Sikh funerals and Kirtan Sohila follow the index for day 786; confirm phrasing 'going home'.

Editor: hook's 'close to two months' replaced with 'for weeks now' (count not in a cited text); Sikh 'evening prayer' corrected to the bedtime prayer, Kirtan Sohila (Rehras is the evening prayer, used on day 814). Day 816 now has a script; review matches it.

Audit: 'a Buddhist teacher and a Christian priest aren't giving two versions of one answer' was stated as fact by the narrator; reframed as this path's way of reading them, since some readers (perennialists) do hold the answers converge.
